title: Facile synthesis of SnSe–MnTe nanocomposite as a promising electrode for supercapacitor applications

predicted_errors.error_location: Results and Discussion — GCD numerical values (Cs=1502 F/g, SE=61.05 Wh/kg, SP=270.5 W/kg at 1.0 A/g)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The three key performance metrics reported at 1.0 A/g are mutually inconsistent when verified against the paper's own equations. Using the stated potential window ΔV=0.65 V and eqn (5) Cs=I×Δt/(m×ΔV), the discharge time Δt = 1502×0.65 = 976.3 s. From eqn (6) SE=Cs×ΔV²/7.2, the calculated specific energy is 1502×0.4225/7.2 = 88.14 Wh/kg — a 30.7% discrepancy from the reported 61.05 Wh/kg. From eqn (7) SP=Ed×3600/Δt, with the reported SE=61.05 Wh/kg, the calculated SP is 61.05×3600/976.3 = 225.1 W/kg — a 20.2% discrepancy from the reported 270.5 W/kg. Working backwards, the SE value of 61.05 Wh/kg implies a capacitance of only ~1040 F/g, not 1502 F/g. Similarly, the SP value of 270.5 W/kg implies a discharge time of ~812.5 s, not the 976.3 s derived from the reported capacitance. These three values (Cs, SE, SP) cannot all be simultaneously correct under the paper's own formulations (eqns 5–7) with the stated potential window of 0–0.65 V.

predicted_errors.error_location: Equation 3 — Specific capacitance from CV (Section 2.5, Electrochemical measurements)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Equation (3) as presented — Cs = ∫(I×dV)/(m×S×ΔV) — contains a dimensional analysis error. The numerator has units A·V (current × voltage). The denominator has units g × cm² × V (mass × area × voltage). The resulting units are A/(g×cm²), which is not F/g (specific capacitance). The correct standard formula for specific capacitance from cyclic voltammetry is Cs = ∫ I dV / (m × ν × ΔV), where ν is the scan rate (V/s). With the correct formula, units are A·s/g = C/g = F/g. The inclusion of S (geometric electrode area in cm²) in the denominator produces incorrect dimensionality and would yield numerically wrong capacitance values if used as written. Note: there is a separate areal capacitance formula (eqn 4) that properly uses S in the denominator for computing F/cm², suggesting a possible conflation of specific and areal capacitance formulations in eqn (3).

predicted_errors.error_location: Chemical reaction equations (1) and (2) — Section 2.2 (Synthesis of MnTe and SnSe)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Both chemical reaction equations (1) MnCl₂ + Te + 2KOH + H₂O → MnTe + 2KCl + H₂O and (2) SnCl₂ + Se + 2KOH + H₂O → SnSe + 2KCl + H₂O are not correctly balanced. H₂O appears on both the reactant and product sides with identical stoichiometry (1:1), yet the KOH on the reactant side contributes additional O and H atoms. Specifically, equation (1) has 3 oxygen atoms and 4 hydrogen atoms on the left but only 1 oxygen and 2 hydrogen on the right. All other elements (Mn, Sn, Te, Se, Cl, K) are balanced. While simplified reaction schemes are common in materials synthesis papers, the inclusion of H₂O as both reactant and product without adjusting for the oxygen/hydrogen from KOH makes these equations stoichiometrically incorrect as written.

summary: Verification of 'Facile synthesis of SnSe–MnTe nanocomposite as a promising electrode for supercapacitor applications' (J. Phys. Chem. Solids, 2024) in exhaustive mode with lenient strictness detected 3 errors requiring attention. Two high-confidence findings (confidence ≥ 0.90) constitute significant issues: (1) The three key performance metrics — specific capacitance (1502 F/g), specific energy (61.05 Wh/kg), and specific power (270.5 W/kg) — are mutually inconsistent when checked against the paper's own equations (5–7). The discrepancies are 30.7% for specific energy and 20.2% for specific power, meaning at least one of these headline values cannot be correct. (2) Equation (3) for computing specific capacitance from CV data has a dimensional analysis error — it includes geometric electrode area S in the denominator, which produces incorrect units. A third medium-confidence finding notes that chemical reaction equations (1) and (2) are not stoichiometrically balanced for oxygen and hydrogen. Given the two high-confidence findings, the paper requires correction of either the reported numerical values or the potential window specification, and revision of equation (3) to the standard formulation. The chemical equation balance should also be addressed in any revision.
